name: Bengaluru fort heritage walk
description: Discover the history of the Bengaluru fort on this walk. The Fort though today reduced to a mere fraction of its original expanse—less than 5%—remains one of the most significant remnants of the city’s pre-colonial past. This heritage walk invites you to step into the vestiges of a fort that once bore witness to battles transitions of power architectural ingenuity and political resilience.The fort began as a modest mud structure before being fortified with stone during Hyder Ali’s rule and later expanded under his son Tipu Sultan. These walls though weathered by time preserve within them the layered narratives of a growing urban center and the complexities of South Indian resistance to British expansion.A highlight of the walk is the iconic Tipu Sultan’s Summer Palace a rare example of Indo-Islamic architecture with its intricate wooden pillars frescoes and elegant symmetry. Once the seat of royal administration and leisure the palace offers insights not only into architectural aesthetics but also into the socio-political life of the Sultanate in the 18th century.As we navigate the narrow lanes of Old Bengaluru one encounters a little-known but historically important site: a surviving armoury tucked into the urban sprawl and forgotten by modern maps. Used during Tipu’s reign this structure is a physical testament to the city’s martial past and the strategic importance of Bangalore in Mysore’s military planning.A focal point of this walk is the Battle of Bangalore (1791) a critical campaign during the Third Anglo-Mysore War. The battle pitted the British East India Company against Tipu Sultan’s forces and highlighted not only the military prowess of the Sultanate but also broader geopolitical shifts—especially the fallout of British actions in other global theatres such as in the American Revolutionary War.It is particularly notable that the Mysorean rockets used innovatively during this time caught the attention of British military observers. Some of these designs later found their way into documentation that would influence the development of European—and even American—military technology. Legend holds that they partly inspired Francis Scott Key’s reference to "the rockets' red glare" in the Star-Spangled Banner.Finally the walk concludes with a return to the present—by way of South Indian culinary tradition offering participants a curated local snack and a cup of filter coffee. A reminder that history does not only reside in books or ruins—it lives on in tastes traditions and memories.This walking tour is not just about stones and structures. It is a curated window into Bengaluru’s transformation—from fortified stronghold and seat of regional power to colonial outpost and finally to modern metropolis. In walking its paths we do not merely observe history; we retrace it.Note : "This walk is led by a Bengaluru native and professional architect who has lived and studied in the vicinity of the fort for over three decades. His deep-rooted connection to the area combined with his architectural expertise gives him an intimate knowledge of not just every corner of the fort but also the rich history that surrounds it."

name: Kalighat Painting Workshop
description: KALIGHAT PAINTINGS – WHERE TRADITION MEETS MODERNITYBengal is renowned for its rich cultural heritage and diverse artistic traditions, including music, literature, dance, and visual arts. In this workshop, we will explore one of Bengal's most fascinating and thought-provoking art forms—Kalighat Paintings.Bold, expressive & vibrant, Kalighat paintings beautifully bring together a variety of themes, ranging from Hindu mythology and spirituality to secular life and social commentary.Originating in 19th-century Kolkata during the colonial period, this distinctive art form developed around the Kalighat Temple, dedicated to Goddess Kali. The paintings were traditionally created on patas (cloth or paper scrolls) by artists known as Patuas. Located near the banks of the Hooghly River and the popular Kalighat Temple, the area attracted pilgrims, locals, and foreign visitors, creating a thriving audience for these unique artworks.However, with the growing popularity of printed reproductions in the early 20th century, traditional handmade Kalighat paintings gradually declined.The legacy of this expressive art form was later reinterpreted and celebrated by renowned Indian artist Jamini Roy, who drew inspiration from Bengal's folk traditions and brought a distinctive modern interpretation to traditional Indian art.What will you learn?Learn about the history and evolution of Kalighat PaintingsExplore the life and artistic journey of Jamini RoyUnderstand the distinctive themes, styles, and visual language of this art formDiscover how traditional Indian folk art influenced modern artistic expressionCreate your very own Kalighat-inspired paintingThis will be a wonderful opportunity to experience Indian art and culture through storytelling, learning, and hands-on creativity!Note:All art materials required for the workshop will be provided by the host.What will you take home?A Detailed Hands-On Workshop WorkbookKnowledge & History of Kalighat art & cultureYour very own completed artwork created during the workshopWhat do you need to bring?A water bottle to keep yourself hydrated.All workshop materials will be provided. However, if preferred, you may bring an examination pad or paper board for additional support while working.Please NoteKindly be on time, Participants arriving late may miss the storytelling and introduction to the history of this beautiful art form.No refunds will be provided for cancellations.Come, explore the vibrant world of Kalighat Paintings, where storytelling, tradition, culture, and creativity come together & take home a beautiful piece of art created by you!

name: Mycelium and Muse - Interactive Science Class
description: We often equate creativity with making art. Picasso was creative. Beethoven was creative. Van Gogh was creative.But what about the person who first picked up a piece of charcoal and scribbled on the wall of a cave, hoping the people in the next cave would get the message? Or the bowerbird who spends an entire season collecting blue bottle caps and flowers to decorate a little stage for a mate?And what about a fungus? This one is literally brainless, yet it sends out electrical signals that, when connected to a synthesizer, play out like music.So if creativity shows up in organisms without brains, it is far older than us, isn't it? That's the question we'll sit with over coffee: where creativity really begins on the tree of life, and what that means for those of us who have spent years saying "I'm just not the creative type."Along the way, you'll hear a mushroom play music, and you'll make something that is deliberately, wonderfully bad. You don't need any science background to join in.Just come, grab a coffee, and let's get some creativity brewing. Because, tell you what, I'm not sure a creative life is a happier one. But I'm pretty sure it's a far more meaningful one.About the Speaker:Bitasta Datta is a microbiologist by training, an educator by profession and a science storyteller by passion.For over 10 years, she has been turning science into stories for school learners and curious adults. She started at the National Digital Library of India, went on to co-found The Synapse, led curriculum and learning experience design at BYJU'S and Tutopiya, and tinkers with content at Khan Academy.

description: BhimaSunday, 22nd November, 6.00 p.m. - 7.10 p.m.Language: EnglishAbout the PerformanceDrawing inspiration from Ashok Malhotra’s Child Man, MT Vasudevan Nair’s Randamoozham, and Jeanette Winterson’s Weight, this play explores the paradoxes and ironies in the life of the second Pandava, Bhima.Who is Bhima? name: The Death of Galileo
description: The Death of GalileoWednesday, 25th November, 7.30 p.m. - 8.50 p.m.Language: HindiAbout the PerformanceThis play is an adaptation of Bertolt Brecht’s Life of Galileo. Using a non-linear theatrical structure, it connects Galileo’s struggle to contemporary realities.The play unfolds at night inside a museum, where a group arrives to demolish its collection of cultural and collective living memories and objects. Among the artefacts, they discover a telescope, which becomes the point of departure for the story of Galileo — his discoveries, struggles, confinement and unceasing search for truth. As the night progresses, Galileo’s time and the present time begin to unfold simultaneously, revealing parallels between social realities in two different historical moments.The members of the demolition group are themselves caught between disillusionment, violence and self-deception. Their encounter with the museum and with Galileo stirs their conscience, and while one group remains adamant, the other begins to question its reasons for wanting to destroy the museum. An internal conflict begins, between the path they’ve chosen, to raze the museum for their pride, and the path their conscience wants to guide them towards. Experimental music anchors the play in the present moment, voicing the characters' contradictions and a call to act for co-existence.The performance draws on Brecht’s distancing effect alongside character expression, an actor-development process emerging from Rajkumar Rajak’s research.CastGalileo Galilei: Ramratan GugaliaAndrea and Roman Pope: Mohit VaishnavVihan and Barberini (Narrator): Adnan KhanYoginder and Hitler: Aftab NoorVijay and Sipahi: Ashish DhapBalveer and Roman Sanyasi: Chitaranjan NamaDhyan and Astronomer: Karan Kumar and Shubham MeghwanshiBruno and Ludovico: Aman TaseraBruno’s Mother and Hamid’s Mother: Raina Raha RajakPeople of Rome and Chorus: Rajwanti Tamoli, Vijaylaxmi Tasera, Niana Raha, Ayush KesarwaniCrewDirector: Rajkumar RajakMusic Design and Composition: Garvit GidwaniMusic Assistants: Aman Tasera, Chitaranjan Nama and Harmendra SartaajLighting Design and Operation: Ravi Kumar Pathak and Harmendra SartaajCostume Design: Shubham Meghwanshi, Raina Raha Rajak and Aftab NoorProps Design: Firoz AlamProduction Managers: Raina Raha and MohitProduction Supervision: Ajeet BahadurProduced by: Ex-tra An Organisation and Community Theatre TonkAbout the ArtistsRajkumar RajakRajkumar Rajak is a theatre artist whose practice connects theatre with education and with communities. His artistic journey has been shaped by a persistent curiosity about the relationship between the actor’s body, mind and emotions, their socialisation, and how these shape their character and performance. Much of his theatre practice has grown through working with non-actors from rural and small-town communities who, through sustained engagement in his productions, have evolved as actors and, in some cases, developed their own content and language of theatre.Rajkumar has been finding his own pathways for actor development through experimental rehearsal processes. His practice-based research, Actorgy, explores the actor as a social-historical body and the development of character through relationships, interaction and performance. His directorial work includes Suraj Ka Satwaan Ghoda, Hawalaat, Bhukhwasi Bhand and The Death of Galileo.He worked with the Azim Premji Foundation as a teacher educator for twelve years, and designed its Arts Education Internship. He has also received a new performance grant from the India Foundation for the Arts (2009-10), and the Ministry of Culture’s Junior Research Fellowship 2014.Ramratan GugaliaRamratan Gugulia has been engaged in theatre for the past 10 years as an actor, lyricist and director. He has since performed a range of roles in Bade Bhai Sahab, Jyoti, Nirantar Eklavya, Tonk Junction, Visarjan and Dakghar, and he has taken part in leading theatre festivals such as Jairangam and Bharat Rang Mahotsav. As a director, he has adapted and staged Rabindranath Tagore’s story Tota. Every summer vacation, he volunteers as a facilitator in children’s theatre workshops run by Community Theatre Tonk. He believes that theatre is a space where ideas can be reflected on and practised until they become part of everyday life, rather than remaining as talk of what “should be done”. A government school teacher by profession, he teaches language to children. description: Goonj ka GharThursday, 26th November, 7.30 p.m. - 8.20 p.m.Language: Hindi (with subtitles in English)About the PerformanceGoonj ka Ghar is a physical theatre performance that combines movement, minimal set design, and fragmented storytelling to explore themes of identity, power, and marginalisation. Initially inspired by three seminal short stories, Tirichh by Uday Prakash, Toba Tek Singh by Saadat Hasan Manto, and Uljhan by Vijaydan Detha, which are woven into a single theatrical narrative that interrogates unresolved questions of identity, belonging and justice in today’s world.Set against the backdrop of a society grappling with citizenship, identity and social justice, the performance raises urgent questions: What makes a person a citizen? What do we call home when borders both physical and psychological remain in flux? Who is considered sane, worthy, beautiful, or legitimate? Why does society continue to value women who appear silent and submissive? name: Kadambari: Tracing Fragments of a Shattered Muse
description: Kadambari: Tracing Fragments of a Shattered MuseFriday, 27th November, 7.30 p.m - 9.00 p.m.Language: Hindi, BengaliAbout the PerformanceKadambari is a lyrical theatrical journey into the silenced life of Kadambari Devi, Rabindranath Tagore’s critic, muse, companion, and sister-in-law, married into the Tagore household at nine and gone by 25, when the poet himself was only 23. Rather than reducing her to a footnote in his biography, the play seeks to restore her voice, weaving memory, fiction and imagination. name: How Not to Build a Theatre Institution
description: How Not to Build a Theatre InstitutionA Conversation with Abhishek Mudgal, Sanyukta Saha and Abhishek Majumdar, moderated by Priyanka Varma Friday, 27th November, 5.00 p.m. - 6.30 p.m.About the ConversationArtists establish and lead theatre institutions (which include long-standing initiatives) for different reasons — to practice, teach, present, advocate or support the art form, for instance.But such undertakings, especially if they function independently of secure government or corporate largesse, can falter or fail. The poverty of infrastructure and support for the theatre are among the external factors that are adduced for the precariousness of artist-led institutions. Internal factors are rarely cited. What if the institution is over-reliant on personal equations and goodwill for its sustenance? Or if its ownership is narrowly concentrated in one or two charismatic personalities? Or if it is too obsessed with legacy concerns to avert obsolescence in a swiftly changing environment?This session will investigate what might lie inside any theatre institution that could threaten its stability and hamper its growth. Reflecting on their personal experience of founding and running institutions, three theatre artists will tell us about what worked or did not work about the choices they made. Were discontents allowed to simmer, tensions swept under the carpet or challenges left unaddressed? In hindsight, do they regret any missteps or wish they had done some things differently?About the Participants Sanyukta SahaSanyukta Saha is a theatre pedagogue, facilitator and community arts leader, and the Founder and Executive Director of Aagaaz Theatre Trust, a community-rooted arts organisation in New Delhi. name: Tradition and Modernity in Contemporary Theatre
description: Tradition and Modernity in Contemporary Theatre A Conversation with Sharanya Ramprakash, Laya N Kumar and Parshathy J Nath, moderated by Lakshmana KP Saturday, 28th November, 4.30 p.m. - 6.00 p.m.About the ConversationThe traditions with which contemporary urban Indian theatre artists can engage are immense, embracing mythologies, folk tales and performances, art and craft objects and practices, festivals and rituals, cuisine, inherited knowledge and skills, and much else besides. At the same time, the distinction between the traditional and the modern is not clearcut. Modern theatre in India has a history that stretches back for over two centuries — long enough to develop its own traditions. Dance forms now regarded as ‘classical’ acquired modern practices of teaching, performance and patronage in the last century.The theatre artists in this session will speak about their idea of tradition and how they have interacted with it in the plays they have written, directed or performed. They will also be invited to discuss ethical and political questions that come to the fore when tradition is brought into contemporary theatre work. Has their work been sensitive to the claim that borrowing from inherited forms of expression can constitute a form of cultural theft or disrespects localised and context-specific creation of value and meaning? How would they negotiate with traditions that have been invented in response to market demands or political pressures? Has their work reconciled with, or has it offered a critical perspective on the feudalism, casteism and gender discrimination embedded in many traditional performances and stories?About the ParticipantsSharanya Ramprakash Sharanya Ramprakash is a Bengaluru-based theatre-maker. She places her work at the intersection of gender, tradition and language. She writes, acts, directs and collaborates with a range of forms, communities and theatre-makers across local, national and international locations. Her work is research-based, collaborative and exploratory. She is a member of the Lincoln Centre Director’s Lab, New York. She is also a recipient of the Shankar Nag Theatre Award 2022.Parshathy J NathParshathy J Nath is a theatre artist based in Bengaluru. description: Experience Sharing by Dr Sahana PinjarLecture-Demonstration on the Folk Theatre of BayalataMonday, 23rd November, 7.00 p.m. - 8.00 p.m.About the SessionDr. Sahana Pinjar will be presenting a live demonstration of the traditional Kannada folk-theatre form of Bayalata through the performance of Girija Kalyana, depicting the divine marriage of Girija (Parvati) and Lord Shiva. The demonstration will showcase the storytelling, acting, dialogue, traditional movements, music, costumes, and theatrical conventions of Bayalata, bringing the story to life for a contemporary audience. The story, written by Dr. Basavaraja Malshati, portrays Girija’s deep devotion and determination to attain Lord Shiva, her penance, and the eventual divine wedding. Through lively characters, expressive acting, traditional music and the energetic style of Bayalata, the narrative unfolds as both a sacred tale and a vibrant theatrical experience. The performance celebrates themes of devotion, love, perseverance and the union of divine energies, while preserving the distinctive visual and performative elements of Karnataka’s folk theatre tradition.CastGirija and Rathi: Dr. Sahana PinjarShiva: Syed Sadiq SManmatha: Nehar AhamadaSutradhara: Anklesh HSarathi: K NagarajMusicTabla: GadhlingappaHarmonium: EraswamiAbout the ArtistsDr. Sahana PinjarA dedicated theatre practitioner, researcher, and CCRT Senior Fellow, Sahana‘s creative practice spans grassroots cultural documentation, indigenous folk traditions, and community-engaged arts. name: Mycelium & Muse: A Science Storytelling Workshop
description: About the Workshop:We often equate creativity with making art. Picasso was creative. Beethoven was creative. Van Gogh was creative.But what about the person who first picked up a piece of charcoal and scribbled on the wall of a cave, hoping the people in the next cave would get the message? Or the bowerbird who spends an entire season collecting blue bottle caps and flowers to decorate a little stage for a mate?And what about a fungus? This one is literally brainless, yet it sends out electrical signals that, when connected to a synthesiser, play out like music.So if creativity shows up in organisms without brains, it is far older than us, isn't it?That's the question we'll sit with: Where does creativity really begin on the tree of life, and what does that mean for all of us who have spent years saying "I'm just not the creative type". Along the way, you'll hear a mushroom playing music, make an idea card that is deliberately, wonderfully bad, write a letter to your future self, and discover a new answer to the question “Am I creative?”You don't need any science background to join in. Just come in, and let's get some creativity brewing.Because, tell you what, we are not sure if a creative life is a happier one. But what we can absolutely guarantee is that it's a far more meaningful one.About the facilitator:Bitasta Datta is a microbiologist by training, an educator by profession and a science storyteller by passion.For over 10 years, she has been turning science into stories for school learners and curious adults. She started at the National Digital Library of India, went on to co-found The Synapse, led curriculum and learning experience design at BYJU'S and Tutopiya, and now leads the efforts at Khan Academy India to narrate science in a way that sticks.She believes science and art are two lenses on the same world, and that if you look through both long enough, you arrive at the same philosophy. So that's what she does. She dissects science to find the art in it, dissects art to find the science in it, and narrates her findings as stories.Outside work, she paints, bakes, and travels, and writes about the places where science, art and philosophy run into each other. Mycelium & Muse began as one of those pieces.

name: Stage Management
description: Stage ManagementA Three-Day Workshop by Abhishek MudgalThursday to Saturday, 26th to 28th November, 10.00 a.m. - 3.00 p.m.Points to NoteYour place in the workshop will be confirmed only after payment and final selection. If you are not selected, the fee will be refunded.If you are selected and attend the entire workshop, the fee will be refunded.If you are selected and there is a no-show, or if you attend only part of the workshop, there will be no refund.About the WorkshopThis introductory workshop is designed to give participants a practical understanding of the role of a stage manager and the stage management process in theatre.The workshop will introduce participants to terminology and the various departments of theatre, followed by an exploration of the role and responsibilities of a stage manager across the different stages of a production — from pre-production and rehearsals to technical rehearsals and performances.Participants will be introduced to basic stage management paperwork, organisational tools, communication practices and production processes. A key component will be crisis management, where participants will work through real-life theatre situations and learn to approach unexpected challenges with calm, logical and collaborative thinking. The workshop will combine discussions, group activities, practical exercises and demonstrations, providing participants with a strong foundation in stage management.About the FacilitatorAbhishek MudgalA State Sangeet Natak Akademi Awardee, Abhishek Mudgal graduated from the Department of Dramatics, University of Rajasthan. He also holds a Diploma in Natyashastra and Western Theatre from Rabindranath Tagore University, Bhopal.In 2021, he was honoured with the Junior Fellowship by the Ministry of Culture, recognising his sustained contribution to Indian theatre. He has directed and performed in over 1000 street plays on women’s safety across Rajasthan in the aftermath of the Delhi rape case. In 2012, he was awarded the Ministry of Culture’s Scholarship for Young Artists for extensive research on acting styles.Abhishek has directed more than 25 plays, including Hayavadana, Mahabrahman, Raktkalyan, Dulari Bai and Rashmirathi (based on Ramdhari Singh Dinkar’s epic poem).He is the Founder and Director of the Rang Rajasthan Festival, one of India’s leading theatre festivals, which has been running successfully for the past 11 years. He has also served as Programme Officer at Rajasthan International Centre and as Stage Manager at Rajasthan Sangeet Natak Akademi.Currently, Abhishek serves as Stage Manager at the National School of Drama. In 2025, he represented India at the Singapore Indian Theatre Festival, organised by the High Commission of India, Singapore.Applicants to NoteApplicants are required to fill in the form linked below to give us an understanding of their experience, interests and more.Workshop Application Form: Stage ManagementEligibility Age: 18 years and aboveExperience: Participants with an interest in theatre, acting, stagecraft, production, or related performing arts may apply. Prior theatre experience is welcome but not mandatory. Preference may be given to participants who demonstrate commitment, curiosity, openness to collaborative work, and a willingness to actively engage in the Stage Management workshop process.Physical Readiness: Physical fitness is not compulsory. However, participants should be comfortable taking part in some practical, activity-based exercises that may involve movement.Advisory Clothing: Comfortable and loose clothing is recommended, preferably with pockets. Participants may also carry a small bag for essential items.Food Advisory: Participants are advised to avoid having very heavy meals immediately before practical activities.Participants should carry a bottle of water.About the FestivalPLAYINTERPLAY is a theatre festival with a difference. It celebrates 50 years of the Inlaks Shivdasani Foundation, bringing together its theatre awardees and scholars to show their work, share their experiences, skills and learnings, and converse on matters of common interest.PLAYINTERPLAY presents plays that are new to Bengaluru. What is different, however, is that it looks back as well as forward, featuring a work of theatre that has been specially revived for the festival and readings of plays that are still to become the finished article.PLAYINTERPLAY does more: it forges connections between its constituent parts — performances, workshops, conversations and experience sharing — emphasising the interplay between thought, learning and practice.See the plays! Apply for the workshops! Join the conversations! Soak in the magic of theatre.About the Artistic DirectorAnmol Vellani is the founder and former executive director of India Foundation for the Arts, the first independent philanthropic organisation in India devoted exclusively to supporting the arts. He is also the co-founder of Toto Funds the Arts, which nurtures, encourages and rewards new voices and emerging talent in the arts.Anmol did not, however, aspire to become a professional in the field of philanthropy. His early fascination was with the arts, especially theatre and music, and also philosophy, which he studied at the Universities of Poona, Oxford and Cambridge. He taught ethics, logic and the history of philosophy at Elphinstone College, Mumbai, in the 1970s.His writing and talks — on arts entrepreneurship, the creative economy, cultural policy, the role of grant-making foundations, culture and development, arts collaboration and the performing arts, for example — have reflected on the insights he has gleaned from his long engagement with the arts and philanthropy.Anmol has been associated with nearly 50 plays as a director, designer or actor. He has directed theatre productions in different languages and cities. His last two plays — Innocence (2024) and Apne Ghar Jaisa (2022) — have been lauded for their sharp and critical look at contemporary social and political realities in India.

name: Block Party: Construction Play for Children's Day
description: This Children’s Day, Sabha Bengaluru becomes a giant playground for building, making and imagination.Join us on Friday, 13 November and Saturday, 14 November for Block Party — a two-day celebration of open-ended construction play for children and families in Bengaluru.At the heart of the event is Troy Blocks, a collection of 11 simple geometric forms that can be transformed into anything children can imagine. The Flat Roof Building at Sabha will become a large-scale free-play space where children can build, experiment, collaborate, take things apart and start again. There are no instructions, no right or wrong answers, no competition and no finished model to copy.Across the Sabha campus, visitors will discover playful Troy Block installations and unexpected architectural interventions. Tinkernauts will be bringing hands-on making, tinkering and creative building activities for curious young minds.Luna Sole will bring messy and sensory play activities for kids aged 18 months - 4 years, creating  opportunities for our littlest children to explore through making and movement.Block Party will also feature a curated marketplace, food stalls and performances by children. In the evenings, the programme will open up to conversations with architects and designers about creativity, architecture, play and how we imagine and build the world around us.Designed for children, parents and curious grown-ups, Block Party is an invitation to slow down, get hands-on and experience the joy of making something together.Come for an hour or stay for the day. Build something enormous, something unexpected, or something that falls down! BLOCK PARTY13–14 November 2026Sabha BengaluruA Children’s Day celebration of construction play, creativity, architecture and open-ended exploration.

name: Bangalore Readers Community - Saturday Reading Session
description: Welcome to the Reading Session by Bangalore Readers Community!This is a space for people who love to read — not a book club with assigned reading, not a discussion group you're obligated to speak in. Just a quiet, comfortable space to read your own book, surrounded by other readers.What to expect:The first 1.5 hours are for silent reading. Bring any book you're currently reading — fiction, non-fiction, poetry, whatever you're into. Find a comfortable spot, order your breakfast & coffee, and read at your own pace alongside other members.The last 30 minutes are for conversation — entirely optional. If you'd like to talk about what you're reading, you're welcome to do so. Or you can just listen to what others share. No pressure.Come alone or with a friend. Many of our members are meeting fellow readers for the first time — it's a relaxed, low-stakes way to be around people who enjoy books as much as you do.What to bring:Just your book (or e-reader/Kindle). No assigned reading, no reading schedule to catch up on.A few things to know:Entry by RSVP only, no walk-ins allowed.Spots are limited, so an RSVP here reserves your place.The event is free but we encourage you to place a food or drink order at the cafe.Come spend a quiet Saturday morning doing something you probably don't make enough time for — reading, uninterrupted, in good company.And follow us on Instagram here: https://www.instagram.com/bangalorereaderscommunity/See you at the event! 📖

description: THE HEART SONGA celebration of divine love through song, story, music and dance.What happens when the mysticism of Bengal's Baul tradition meets the soul of jazz and the beauty of Indian classical music?The Heart Song brings together two extraordinary artists — Parvathy Baul, an internationally acclaimed Baul practitioner and Sangeet Natak Akademi Award recipient, and George Brooks, a celebrated American saxophonist and composer known for his pioneering collaborations with Indian classical legends including Zakir Hussain and Pt. Hariprasad Chaurasia.Joining them are three exceptional musicians — Ashok Ayengar on sitar, Manjunath Sattyasheel on percussion, and Vaibhav Ramani on violin — each bringing their own rich musical traditions into this beautiful collaboration.Through soulful singing, poetry, storytelling, movement and improvisation, The Heart Song explores love, longing, devotion and our shared search for connection.More than a concert, this is an invitation to slow down, listen deeply and experience music that transcends language, culture and boundaries.Come with an open heart. description: Ghost Story Night is an unscripted storytelling session in which event-goers sign up as either storytellers or listeners. Instead of telling well-known ghost stories, we invite interested audience members to sign up as storytellers and to tell the story that’s been haunting them (à la “Are You Afraid of the Dark,” for any 90s TV fans). To that end, we hope to bring together a variety of people to tell their own ghost stories or stories of people they know, and thus, to reveal something frightening, truthful, and even beautiful about the world we inhabit.

name: Philosophy Cafe - Death
description: What is a Philosophy Cafe?This is a group conversation organized by Useful Philosophy, designed to help you spot the weaknesses in your own certainties. It is low-pressure, high-clarity, and strictly "No Guru". We live in times of "winning" arguments, where we lose finding truth and understanding. If you are tired of shouting matches and looking for a space to actually think out loud, join our Philosophy Cafe for philosophical conversations over brunch.Bring in your questions to philosophize with the group! We put them to a vote and select the most popular question to discuss in the session.We are ditching spiritual cliches and shallow mantras to dive into the dilemmas of modern life. Whether you are curious about why you believe what you believe or just want to enjoy an afternoon of interesting conversations over coffee, this is your ‘third space’ for clarity.This isn't a book club. You don't need to have read a single page of Plato to join. As a group, we will use Socratic questioning to peel back the layers of the topic at hand.What we won't do: ❌ Listen to long rambles❌ Debate for the sake of "winning"❌ Speak in academic jargonWhat we will do: ✅ Ask good questions✅ Challenge the "obvious"✅ Drink good coffeeWhat's new:+ Theme for this session: DeathExample Qs:Why do we dread the nonexistence after death, yet feel indifferent about the nonexistence before our birth?Would immortality make human life meaningless?When we grieve, are we mourning for the dead or for ourselves?+ A brief on the theme by Sayli+Early RSVP open for members on the Whatsapp broadcast list to prioritize spots for regulars--------------About the facilitator: Sayli is someone who lives in between life and death and a self-identified weirdo.About the organizer: Basit Manham is a philosophical counselor at Manham Philosophical Consulting and runs Useful Philosophy - We rescue useful ideas from philosophy books and make them accessible to all.

name: Ritu Raga Rang: Seasons through Ragas
description: Ritu Raga Rang: Seasons through RagasThe world of Hindustani classical music has been traditionally linked to the idea of seasons. Ancient Indian scriptures described six distinct seasons or ritus: Vasant (Spring), Grishma (summer), Varsha (monsoon), Sharad (Autumn), Hemant (Pre-Winter) and Shishir (Winter). Each of these seasons bring about different moods and feelings. In this multi-sensory performance, which includes Ragamala paintings and fragrances that evoke the feelings of each season, Nishant will paint portraits of the ritus using ragas and compositions as a canvas. This programme premiered at Stanford University to a warm reception and now comes to Bengaluru for the first time.Nishant is accompanied by Sri Udayaraj Karpur on tabla and Sri Surya Upadhyaya on harmonium.The concert is set in Sabha, a restored 160-year-old building in Shivaji Nagar, an intimate space well suited to a baithak-style evening of khayal.About the artistNishant Panicker is a Hindustani vocalist of the Agra-Atrauli gharana and a disciple of the late Vidushi Lalith J. Rao. He received his early training from the late sarod maestro Pandit Rajeev Taranath. At 15 he was a finalist in Naad Bhed, the national classical music talent search by SPIC MACAY and Doordarshan, and at 18 he was among the youngest recipients of the NCPA Hindustani Vocal Scholarship. He has performed at many prestigious venues across India and USA including the NCPA Mumbai, India International Centre Delhi, Bharat Bhavan Bhopal, Bangalore International Centre, Chowdiah Memorial Hall, Stanford University, Chinmaya Amarnath Pittsburgh and the Chhandayan Center in New York. He is also a regular performer in the music collective Sunaad.Facebook | Youtube | Insta

name: unLecture x Gully Labs Bangalore
description: Five very different conversations. One very curious city.Bangalore, we're here!! And we're bringing you five sessions that go from the psychology of power to the politics of citizenship, from economics that turns everything you thought you knew on its head to robots dreaming of Mars, and poetry that asks what it means to keep feeling things in a world that can be a little too much.We're revisiting one of psychology's most famous experiments, questioning who gets to belong in a democracy, finding out why good intentions can make terrible policies, meeting the robots that could one day assist astronauts, and spending an evening with poetry, power, and pleasure.Basically, a little psychology, a little politics, a little science, and a lot of things to think about long after you leave.31st October: The Stanford Prison Experiment: Who Gave You That Power?Ganga M NairThe experiment lasted six days. The legend got a life sentence. We all know the story of ordinary people given power and what supposedly happened next. But what does the experiment actually tell us about human behaviour? And how does power show up in our group chats, relationships, family lunches, and Monday meetings? Through behavioural psychology, neuroscience, and a few experiments on ourselves, we'll unpack the power dynamics hiding in plain sight.1st November: SIR and the Crisis of Documentary CitizenshipAdil HossainWhat does it mean to belong to a country, and who gets to decide? Looking at the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls through the lens of documentary citizenship, political anthropologist Adil Hossain examines how documents, identity, religion, and ideas of belonging shape who gets recognised as a citizen — and who risks being excluded.14th November: The Counter-Intuitive Economist: Stories About Why Good Intentions Make Bad PolicyAnupam ManurIs a cotton tote really better for the planet than a plastic bag? Are higher prices during a disaster always a bad thing? And why do attempts to cut out middlemen so often fail? Professor Anupam Manur takes us through the economic ideas hiding behind everyday assumptions, using stories that challenge what we think we know. No equations, no jargon, just a few surprises about how the world works.22nd November: VLA Rovers: From Assistive Household Companions to Mars ExplorationPradipta BoseWhat if a robot could understand what you say, see the world around it, and figure out what to do next? From assistive technologies that translate eye movements into actions to intelligent rovers designed for the challenges of space, Prof. Pradipta Bose explores how vision-language-action models are changing the way humans and robots work together — on Earth and potentially on Mars.28th November: Zulmaton ke Daur Mein: An Evening of Poetry, Power, and PleasureNeha MishraWhat is the point of poetry in a world that often seems determined to do without it? From Plato's attempts to banish poetry from his Republic to contemporary attempts to regulate art and literature, this session explores why poetry continues to matter. Through a selection of poems, we'll think about emotion, pleasure, politics, and how reading might help us find our way through the overwhelming despair of our times.Five sessions, five different rabbit holes, and hopefully a whole lot of new questions.Bangalore, come curious. Leave with something to think about.
